lawyer:
Khalilur Rahman with Rubaiyat Hossain, Advocates ------ For the Petitioners. 
Md Nesar Ahmed with Md Nurul Huda, Advocates ------ For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Chairman, Uttara Management Ltd and ors ------ Petitioners
Vs.
Chairman, Labour Court, Rajshahi and another ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Awlad Ali J: This Rule arises out of an order dated 31-3-1998 deciding the question of jurisdiction of the Labour Court and also the judgment dated 4-8-1998 passed by the Labour Court, Rajshahi in Complaint Case No. 4/97. 

 2. Briefly stated, the facts are that the respondent No. 2 Md Jamaluddin filed Complaint Case No. 4/97 under section 25(1)(b) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act. 1965 in the Labour Court at Rajshahi asserting. inter alia, that he joined Aziz Match Factory in 1963 as a Box Filler and was made permanent in the said post in 1965. After liberation of Bangladesh the said establishment was taken over by the Government of Bangladesh as an abandoned industry. The petitioner was promoted to the post of Checker in the rank of a senior worker and then in 1978 the said factory was sold to private ownership that is. to the petitioner No. 1, namely, Uttara Management Ltd and since then the respondent No. 2 had been working under the petitioner No.3. In consideration of his satisfactory performance he was promoted to the post of Senior Supervisor. While he was performing his duties as such he was charged for his misconduct by letter dated 16-2-1997 and he was placed under suspension and asked to show cause within 3 days as to why he should not be dismissed from service for the misconduct. The respondent No. 2 submitted the explanation and prayed for absolving him from the charge but the petitioner No.3 constituted an inquiry committee by order dated 2-3-1997 and asked the respondent No. 2 to attend the Inquiry Committee on 8-3-1997. He attended before the Inquiry Committee and the Inquiry Committee submitted a report and on the basis of the report the petitioner No.3 vide his order dated 16-4-1997 dismissed the respondent No. 2 from service. Thereafter, the respondent No. 2 submitted a grievance petition on 26-4-1997 by registered post and having failed to get any favourable response filed the Complaint Case No. 4/97 in the Labour Court, Rajshahi praying for his reinstatement with back wages and other costs. 

 3. The petitioner No. 2 contested the complaint case by filing written statement stating, inter alia, that the complaint case is not maintainable and the respondent No.2 was a Senior Supervisor and does not fall with the definition of worker as per section 2(v)(ii) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965, and further claimed that both the Chairman and the Managing Director of Uttara Management Ltd have their office at Dhaka at GK Bhaban, 8th Floor, 30, VIP Road, Kakrail, Dhaka and, as such, the complaint case comes within the jurisdiction of the 2nd Labour Court. Dhaka and it does not fall within the territorial jurisdiction of Labour Court, Rajshahi. The respondent No.2 was found with the workers of Box Filling section and he put pressure upon the management in connection with payment of wages and Eid bonus on 8-2-1997 and for causing loss of the Company's property charge was framed under section 17(3) of the Act and he was asked to show cause within 3 days as required under the law and the reply of the respondent No.2 was not satisfactory and the matter was inquired into by three-member Inquiry Committee in which charge was established. His service record was also found to be unsatisfactory and, as such, he was dismissed from service in a lawful manner by the order dated 16-4-1997. The petitioner No. 3 by filing an application raised objection with regard to territorial jurisdiction of Rajshahi Labour Court to entertain the complaint case and the Labour Court after hearing by order dated 31-3-1998 rejected the plea of the petitioner as to the question of jurisdiction and proceeded with the case fixing 3-5-1998 for final hearing. The Labour Court, Rajshahi after hearing the parties and considering the evidence adduced, by the impugned Judgment dated 4-8-1998 allowed the complaint case and ordered for reinstatement of the respondent No. 2 with back wages by setting aside the order of dismissal dated 16-4-1997. 

 4. Respondent No. 2 has filed affidavit-in-opposition contending, inter alia, that the respondent No. 2 had no managerial or administrative function and he had been a technical and skilled hand, as such, the management dealt with him and treated him as a worker under the provision of Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965. The respondent No.2 worked in Aziz Match Factory situated at Rajshahi and charge- sheet was issued there and thereafter the order of dismissal was passed by the Manager (Co- Ordination) of the said Aziz Match Factory and Rajshahi Labour Court has territorial jurisdiction and rightly rejected the application of the petitioner No. 3 for dismissal of the case on the ground of maintainability. It has further been contended that while awarding the extreme penalty of dismissal from service the respondent No. 2 had not been heard in person by the petitioner employer and his attention was not drawn to the incriminating evidence to counter allegations and that in the order of dismissal also there is no specific incriminating materials. The inquiry was a perverse one and the Labour Court, Rajshahi came to the conclusion that the Inquiry. Committee did not act legally and properly and in the inquiry report the charge against the respondent No.2 had not at all been established. 

 5. Mr Khalilur Rahman, representing the petitioners, pointing out clause (g) of section 17 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and also section 18 of the said Act has contended that the charge was brought against the respondent No.2 for misconduct committed in the factory and that allegation was brought against him that was recorded in writing and communicated to him and also he was given 3 days time to explain and that he had been given personal hearing, as it appears from the record in the complaint case, and that requirement of law having been fulfilled as regards bringing the charge and making an inquiry by a properly constituted Inquiry Committee. the order of dismissal is a valid one, and that under section 25(d) of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 the Labour Court in appropriate case may make an order for reinstatement of the complainant. According to him, the case of the complainant was not an appropriate case as he misconducted as defined under clause (g) of section 17 of the Act. The next contention of Mr Khalilur Rahman is that the Rajshahi Labour Court had no territorial jurisdiction to entertain the petition of complaint as the concurrent jurisdiction was prescribed under SRO No. 101-L/80-LlWVI/1(1)78 which provided for the cases falling within the concurrent jurisdiction of more than one Labour Court only the 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka would assume the jurisdiction in deciding the case and since the factory was situated within the jurisdiction of Rajshahi Labour Court and the Head Office of the complainant situated admittedly in Dhaka the case apparently fell in two jurisdictions both at Rajshahi and Dhaka and in that case 2nd Labour Court, Dhaka is competent to entertain the petition of complaint. He has referred to the case of Md Mahmudul Hoque vs Md Shamsul Alam reported in 36 DLR (AD) 179 where referring the SRO as stated hereinbefore it has been observed in paragraph 4 to effect that, 

 " It is thus clear that the case fell within the concurrent jurisdiction of Labour Court, Rajshahi and Chittagong. Section 35 says that the Government by notification in the Official Gazette, may establish as many Labour Courts as it considers necessary and where it establishes more than one Labour Court, shall, specify in the Notification the territorial limits within which each one of them shall exercise jurisdiction under the Ordinance. The law itself mentioned its territorial limits for exercising jurisdiction and therefore, when a Labour Court exercises jurisdiction which is beyond its territorial limits, that exercise of jurisdiction is void and without jurisdiction and consequently, the proceedings are also void", 

 6. Mr Md Nesar Ahmed, representing the respondent No. 2, on the other hand, has contended that the very charge was framed under section 17 treating the respondent No. 2 as worker and that he was also dismissed by the petitioner according to the provision of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act, 1965 and the petitioners cannot now say that respondent No. 2 is not a worker. Pointing out the definitive clause (v)(ii) of section 2 he has submitted that although the respondent No. 2 after promotion had been performing his duty as Senior Supervisor but having regard to the nature of his duty attached to the office he cannot be termed as Manager or Administrator and that he was not functioning in the managerial or administrative capacity. In support of this submission of the learned Advocate he has placed reliance in the case of Senior Manager. Dosta Textile Mills LId vs Sudhansu Bikash Nath reported in 40 DLR (AD) 45 = 52 DLR (AD) 45 where quoting section 2(v) it has been observed in paragraph 7 that. 

 In the case of Pioneer Garments Ltd vs Md Abul Kalam Azad and another reported in 2000 BLD (AD) 62 paragraph 7 the decision reported in 40 DLR (AD) 45 has been referred. Mr Nesar Ahmed next contended that by notification dated 22nd April, 1980 the jurisdiction of Labour Court was fixed but in subsequent SRO No. 214 dated 16-6-1994 there is no provision for concurrent jurisdiction. The Jurisdiction of Rajshahi Labour Court has been specifically mentioned in that and Labour Court will have jurisdiction over the entire Rajshahi Division. Therefore, the earlier SRO or the decision on that SRO as asserted by the learned Counsel of the petitioner has no manner of application. 

 7. It appears from the impugned judgment passed by the Labour Court that the petitioner firstly submitted to the jurisdiction of Labour Court, Rajshahi and filed written statement to contest the complaint case and then raised the question of jurisdiction by filing an application which was ultimately decided in favour of the respondent No. 2 by order dated 31-1-1998. That order having not been challenged the petitioner questioned the jurisdiction in a proceeding under Article 102 of the Constitution as they filed written statement to contest the case. Further, it is clearly provided for under the subsequent SRO that the concurrent jurisdiction was no more there in the subsequent SRO. Therefore, the Rajshahi Labour Court rightly exercised the jurisdiction conferred upon it. The Labour Court having regard to the inquiry report Ext Gha found that the charge or allegation brought against the respondent No. 2 has not been established. Such finding of the Labour Court is in accordance with the provision of law. There is no illegality in such finding, as having examined Ext Gha we also find that there is nothing mentioned in the inquiry report about the nature of misconduct and the charge that was brought against the respondent No. 2. In view of the definition as provided under section 2(v) and the decisions cited above the respondent No. 2 was found to be the worker and his petition of complaint is competent before the Labour Court and the charge having not been established and proved the Labour Court in making the order of reinstatement has not committed any error of law apparent on the face of the record and that it had not acted in excess of its jurisdiction. Therefore, there is no merit in this Rule.
